title: Phage Bets on 10,000-Fold Reversion Mutations, First Humanized EBV Antibody
dek: Phages hedge their bets through 10,000-fold reversion mutations in SSRs, humanized EBV antibodies block tumors in vivo, and vaccine efforts advance on multiple fronts.
why: From phage evolution to EBV antibodies to cognitive laziness, one thread connects molecular mechanisms, drug development and science communication. The antibody data in the second half is especially hardcore.
who: Researchers working on phages or antibodies, investors watching EBV vaccine progress, and engineers who want to understand the science communication predicament.
skip: The first half hour of phage detail is fairly basic; for antibody development only, start at 50:44.

points.h: Phages deliberately let some offspring fail
points.body: Jolene introduces a Nature Microbiology paper: homopolymeric nucleotide repeats (SSRs) in phage genes are prone to slippage during replication, causing insertions or deletions that shift the reading frame. This means a fraction of offspring always fail to produce protein normally. This randomness is the basis of bet-hedging: most sequences are adapted to the current environment, but the persistent low-level variants could become survivors once the environment shifts drastically. The population trades a tiny cost for long-term survival capability.

points.h: No need to pre-adapt: reversion mutations are 10,000 times faster
points.body: The paper measured the reversion mutation frequency in SSR regions and found it roughly 10,000 times higher than ordinary point mutations. This order of magnitude means phages can rapidly turn a gene's function on or off within extremely short generations, rather than waiting for a rare point mutation. Jolene emphasizes that this mechanism lets the population avoid pre-adaptation when the environment changes, instead waiting to be selected by the environment through continuously generated diversity.

points.h: T7 has not a single SSR; betting is not standard equipment
points.body: In the Basel phage collection, the T7 genome has no SSRs. Rich comments that T7 is "businesslike," straightforward, without these fancy mechanisms. This highlights that SSRs are not standard equipment for all phages, but an evolutionary strategy of certain lineages in specific ecological niches. Even virulent phages under the same host can have completely different gene organization.

points.h: The hard part of humanization is not the variable region, it's the constant region
points.body: When converting a mouse antibody into a humanized antibody, there is a conflict between the variable region and the constant region, and someone needs to spend years adjusting the constant region to be compatible with the variable region before a therapeutic antibody can be made. Brienne says this was her epiphany moment; she originally did not understand why mice had to be used. Vincent adds that going directly to human antibodies might not find the antibody you want, while the advantage of the mouse platform is that you can screen large numbers of clones and engineer antigens, obtaining the complete B cell clonal diversification process, after which classic hybridoma technology is still needed to obtain monoclonal antibodies.

points.h: After hybridoma screening, only 10 antibodies remain
points.body: The research group immunized mice with recombinant GP350 and GP42, prepared hybridomas, plated 384-well plates, and used antigen-conjugated magnetic beads for high-throughput flow screening, testing binding and infection inhibition ability. Positive clones were subcloned and had heavy/light chain genes sequenced, then recombinant human IgG1 antibodies were expressed. In the end, 2 GP350-binding antibodies and 8 GP42-neutralizing antibodies were obtained. The whole process demonstrates the complete path from animal immunization to recombinant antibodies.

points.h: The antibodies also blocked EBV challenge in vivo
points.body: Human CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells were implanted into two kinds of immunodeficient mice, 500 micrograms of antibody (ATX42-2, ATX350-2, MO1, etc.) was injected intraperitoneally, then EBV was challenged intravenously, and the mice were observed for 11 weeks. Results showed these antibodies could prevent tumor formation, inhibit viral DNA replication and prevent splenomegaly. No EBER-positive cells were detected in the spleens of mice treated with ATX42-2 and MO1. This means human antibodies have a protective effect against EBV challenge in vivo, not just in vitro neutralization.

points.h: Alum-adjuvanted subunit is dead, nanoparticle vaccines are still alive
points.body: The GP350 subunit vaccine with alum adjuvant failed to produce protective immunity in trials; GP42 is conformationally variable, making it hard to induce the right antibodies. But an existing GP350 ferritin nanoparticle vaccine showed safety and immunogenicity in phase 1, with seropositive participants remaining uninfected with EBV up to 540 days. There are also GH/GP42 ferritin nanoparticles and Moderna's mRNA vaccine (containing four antigens) in development. Vincent expressed disappointment that the paper did not try combining GP350 and GP42 antibodies.

points.h: Anti-vaccine may not lack information, but the will to think
points.body: Vincent re-recommends Thinking, Fast and Slow, quoting Joshua Reynolds' famous line: "There is no expedient to which a man will not resort to avoid the real labor of thinking." He believes cognitive economy may partly explain anti-science and anti-vaccine attitudes: deep thinking is energy-consuming, and people tend toward the effortless Type 1 thinking. He immediately follows with "that's laziness, cognitive laziness." This view attributes the science communication predicament to humans' default cognitive mode, rather than a simple lack of information.
